claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) upregulates the NAD+ dependent histone deacetylase Sirtuin 2 (SIRT2).
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) employs plethora of mechanisms to hijack the host defence machinery for its successful survival, proliferation and persistence. Here, we show that Mtb upregulates one of the key epigenetic modulators, NAD+ dependent histone deacetylase Sirtuin 2 (SIRT2)
evidence: Supported by microarray data (Figure 1A), qRT-PCR (Figure 1B), and flow cytometry (Figure 1C and D) showing increased SIRT2 expression following Mtb infection.

claim: Upon Mtb infection, SIRT2 translocates to the nucleus.
source: Here, we show that Mtb upregulates one of the key epigenetic modulators, NAD+ dependent histone deacetylase Sirtuin 2 (SIRT2), which upon infection translocate to the nucleus
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing SIRT2 predominantly localized to the nucleus following Mtb infection as early as 4 hr pi (Figure 2A) and confirmed by immunoblotting at 24 hr pi (Figure 2B).

claim: SIRT2 deacetylates histone H3K18 upon Mtb infection.
source: which upon infection translocate to the nucleus and deacetylates histone H3K18
evidence: Supported by data showing significant increase in H3K18ac levels in infected macrophages treated with AGK2 (SIRT2 inhibitor) (Figure 2C and D).

claim: SIRT2 modulates the host transcriptome leading to enhanced macrophage activation.
source: deacetylates histone H3K18, thus modulating the host transcriptome leading to enhanced macrophage activation
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis showing that Mtb infection led to differential expression of 992 genes, with 578 genes being SIRT2 dependent (Figure 3A), and KEGG pathway analysis showing effects on pathways involved in TB defense (Figure 3B).

claim: In Mtb specific T cells, SIRT2 deacetylates NFκB-p65 at K310.
source: Furthermore, in Mtb specific T cells, SIRT2 deacetylates NFκB-p65 at K310 to modulate T helper cell differentiation.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry showing that SIRT2 deacetylated NFκB p65 subunit at K310 in Mtb-specific CD3+ lymphocytes (Figure 5E).

claim: SIRT2 deacetylation of NFκB-p65 at K310 modulates T helper cell differentiation.
source: Furthermore, in Mtb specific T cells, SIRT2 deacetylates NFκB-p65 at K310 to modulate T helper cell differentiation.
evidence: Supported by data showing that SIRT2 inhibition increased the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines IFNγ and IL17 by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 4N–Q), indicating a shift toward Th1/Th17 response.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT2 restricts the intracellular growth of drug-sensitive strains of Mtb.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT2 restricts the intracellular growth of both drug-sensitive and resistant strains of Mtb
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometric analysis and CFU enumeration showing significantly reduced Mtb growth in peritoneal macrophages treated with AGK2 (Figure 1E and F).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT2 restricts the intracellular growth of drug-resistant strains of Mtb.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT2 restricts the intracellular growth of both drug-sensitive and resistant strains of Mtb
evidence: Supported by data showing AGK2 treatment significantly decreased the bacillary load of MDR as well as XDR strains of TB (Figure 11G–I).

claim: SIRT2 inhibition enhances the efficacy of front line anti-TB drug Isoniazid in the murine model of infection.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT2 restricts the intracellular growth of both drug-sensitive and resistant strains of Mtb and enhances the efficacy of front line anti-TB drug Isoniazid in the murine model of infection.
evidence: Demonstrated by data showing co-treatment of AGK2 and INH significantly decreased the bacterial burden in the lungs as compared to mice treated with either AGK2 or INH alone (Figure 11F).

claim: SIRT2 inhibitor-treated mice display reduced bacillary load.
source: SIRT2 inhibitor-treated mice display reduced bacillary load, decreased disease pathology and increased Mtb-specific protective immune responses.
evidence: Supported by CFU analysis showing bacterial burden was significantly diminished in the lungs, spleen and liver of mice treated with AGK2 (Figure 6E–G).

claim: SIRT2 inhibitor-treated mice display decreased disease pathology.
source: SIRT2 inhibitor-treated mice display reduced bacillary load, decreased disease pathology and increased Mtb-specific protective immune responses.
evidence: Demonstrated by histopathology analysis showing an overall decrease in lung inflammation after SIRT2 inhibition (Figure 6B–D).

claim: SIRT2 inhibitor-treated mice display increased Mtb-specific protective immune responses.
source: SIRT2 inhibitor-treated mice display reduced bacillary load, decreased disease pathology and increased Mtb-specific protective immune responses.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased percentage of CD11b+, CD11c+, CD80+ and MHCII+ cells (Figure 7), increased activation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 8), and prominent increase in IFNγ and IL17 producing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 9).

claim: Among 18 HDACs, SIRT2 and HDAC6 were significantly upregulated in THP1 cells 24 hr post Mtb infection.
source: Among a total of 18 HDACs, SIRT2 and HDAC6 were significantly upregulated whilst SIRT1 and HDAC9 were downregulated (Figure 1A; Mehta et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis data from Mehta et al., 2016 (Figure 1A).

claim: SIRT1 and HDAC9 were downregulated in THP1 cells 24 hr post Mtb infection.
source: Among a total of 18 HDACs, SIRT2 and HDAC6 were significantly upregulated whilst SIRT1 and HDAC9 were downregulated (Figure 1A; Mehta et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis data from Mehta et al., 2016 (Figure 1A).

claim: The increase in SIRT2 expression following Mtb infection is in accordance with a previous report indicating Mtb mediated downregulation of SIRT1.
source: This is in accordance with a previous report indicating the Mtb mediated downregulation of SIRT1 (Cheng et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2017.

claim: AGK2 treatment significantly increased the percentage of apoptotic cells in Mtb-infected macrophages.
source: its treatment significantly increased the percentage of apoptotic cells in Mtb-infected macrophages with a concomitant decrease in the necrotic population (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis showing increased apoptotic cell populations in AGK2-treated infected macrophages (Figure 1L and M).

claim: AGK2 treatment led to a concomitant decrease in the necrotic population in Mtb-infected macrophages.
source: its treatment significantly increased the percentage of apoptotic cells in Mtb-infected macrophages with a concomitant decrease in the necrotic population (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 1L and M).

claim: AGK2 treatment has minimal effect on apoptosis in uninfected macrophages.
source: While AGK2 treatment has minimal effect on uninfected macrophages (Figure 1J and K)
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data (Figure 1J and K).

claim: AGK2 treatment significantly increased intracellular ROS levels following Mtb infection.
source: Interestingly AGK2 treatment also led to a significant increase in the intracellular ROS levels following Mtb infection with minimal effect on uninfected cells (Figure 1N and O).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis using CellROX staining (Figure 1N and O).

claim: AGK2 treatment has minimal effect on intracellular ROS levels in uninfected cells.
source: Interestingly AGK2 treatment also led to a significant increase in the intracellular ROS levels following Mtb infection with minimal effect on uninfected cells (Figure 1N and O).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 1N and O).

claim: Treatment of cells with N-acetyl cysteine significantly decreased the anti-mycobacterial effect of AGK2.
source: Moreover, treatment of cells with an anti-oxidant, N-acetyl cysteine (Bhaskar et al., 2015) significantly decreased the anti-mycobacterial effect of AGK2 (Figure 1P–R)
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU enumeration showing reduced anti-mycobacterial effect when NAC was added (Figure 1P–R).

claim: ROS generation is one of the mechanisms by which SIRT2 inhibition restricts bacillary growth.
source: indicating that ROS generation is one of the mechanisms by which SIRT2 inhibition restricts bacillary growth.
evidence: Inferred from data showing that treatment with anti-oxidant N-acetyl cysteine significantly decreased the anti-mycobacterial effect of AGK2 (Figure 1P–R).

claim: SIRT2 predominantly localized to the nucleus following Mtb infection as early as 4 hr pi.
source: Interestingly, while SIRT2 presence was observed in both the cytosol and the nucleus of uninfected macrophages, SIRT2 predominantly localized to the nucleus following Mtb infection as early as 4 hr pi (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 2A).

claim: SIRT2 migration into the nucleus was confirmed by immunoblotting at 24 hr pi.
source: SIRT2 migration into the nucleus was also confirmed by performing immunoblotting at 24 hr pi (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis of nuclear and cytosolic fractions (Figure 2B).

claim: There was a significant increase in the overall expression of SIRT2 at protein level post Mtb infection.
source: Significant increase in the overall expression of SIRT2 at protein level post Mtb infection correlated, with our qRT-PCR analysis (Figures 1B and 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot (Figure 2B) and qRT-PCR (Figure 1B).

claim: SIRT2 modulates the acetylation levels of histone H3K18 upon infection with Listeria monocytogenes.
source: Since SIRT2 modulates the acetylation levels of histone H3K18 upon infection with Listeria monocytogenes, we analyzed H3K18 acetylation upon Mtb infection and AGK2 treatment in mouse peritoneal macrophages.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on Listeria monocytogenes.

claim: AGK2 treatment had minimal effect on the acetylation levels of H3K18 in uninfected cells.
source: AGK2 treatment had minimal effect on the acetylation levels of H3K18 in uninfected cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot and flow cytometry (Figure 2C and D).

claim: There was a significant increase in H3K18ac levels in infected macrophages treated with AGK2.
source: However, there was a significant increase in H3K18ac levels in infected macrophages treated with AGK2, indicating that Mtb-induced nuclear localization of SIRT2 results in deacetylation of histone H3K18 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot and flow cytometry (Figure 2C and D).

claim: Mtb-induced nuclear localization of SIRT2 results in deacetylation of histone H3K18.
source: indicating that Mtb-induced nuclear localization of SIRT2 results in deacetylation of histone H3K18 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Inferred from data showing significant increase in H3K18ac levels in infected macrophages treated with AGK2 (Figure 2C and D).

claim: α-tubulin is the major cytosolic target of SIRT2 which deacetylates it at lysine-40 to attenuate microtubule stability.
source: α-tubulin is the major cytosolic target of SIRT2 which deacetylates it at lysine-40 to attenuate microtubule stability (North et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to North et al., 2003.

claim: AGK2 treatment led to a comparable increase in the acetylated α-tubulin levels in uninfected and infected macrophages.
source: AGK2 treatment led to a comparable increase in the acetylated α-tubulin levels in uninfected and infected macrophages indicating the presence of cytosolic SIRT2 activity under both the conditions (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis (Figure 2E).

claim: The presence of cytosolic SIRT2 activity is indicated under both uninfected and infected conditions.
source: AGK2 treatment led to a comparable increase in the acetylated α-tubulin levels in uninfected and infected macrophages indicating the presence of cytosolic SIRT2 activity under both the conditions (Figure 2E).
evidence: Inferred from data showing comparable increase in acetylated α-tubulin levels in both conditions (Figure 2E).

claim: Increased nuclear localization of SIRT2 after Mtb infection may contribute to the enhanced acetylated α-tubulin levels in Mtb infected cells as compared to uninfected counterparts.
source: However, increased nuclear localization of SIRT2 after Mtb infection may contribute to the enhanced acetylated α-tubulin levels in the Mtb infected cells as compared to their uninfected counterparts (Figure 2E).
evidence: Inferred from data showing enhanced acetylated α-tubulin levels in infected cells (Figure 2E).

claim: SIRT2 modulates intracellular signaling by manipulating the activation of key Ser/Thr kinases in host cells.
source: SIRT2 modulates intracellular signaling by manipulating the activation of key Ser/Thr kinases in the host cells (Jing et al., 2007; Kosciuczuk et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jing et al., 2007; Kosciuczuk et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018.

claim: Mtb induced phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and p38 was decreased by AGK2 treatment.
source: Interestingly, Mtb induced phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and p38 was decreased by AGK2 treatment (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis (Figure 2F).

claim: SIRT2 influences the intracellular Mtb growth by modulating the host gene expression.
source: Since SIRT2 inhibition strongly influenced the intracellular signaling and histone deacetylation, both of which ultimately lead to changes in cellular gene expression, we hypothesize that SIRT2 influences the intracellular Mtb growth by modulating the host gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from data showing SIRT2 inhibition affects intracellular signaling and histone deacetylation (Figure 2).

claim: AGK2 treatment in uninfected cells did not alter the gene expression in a significant manner.
source: AGK2 treatment in uninfected cells did not alter the gene expression in a significant manner which is consistent with our earlier results wherein no effect on apoptosis, ROS levels, histone deacetylations and cellular signaling was observed in uninfected cells treated with AGK2 (Figures 1K, O, 2D and F).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data and previous experimental results (Figures 1K, O, 2D and F).

claim: AGK2 treatment significantly affected the gene expression profile induced upon Mtb infection.
source: In contrast, AGK2 treatment significantly affected the gene expression profile induced upon Mtb infection.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis showing differential expression of genes (Figure 3A).

claim: Mtb infection led to the differential expression of 992 genes.
source: In total, Mtb infection led to the differential expression of 992 genes which is in agreement with the previous findings (Mehta et al., 2016; Roy et al., 2018).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis and supported by citations to Mehta et al., 2016; Roy et al., 2018.

claim: 578 genes were categorized as SIRT2 dependent.
source: Genes that remained unaltered after AGK2 treatment were categorized as SIRT2 independent (414 genes) and the rest as SIRT2 dependent (578 genes) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis (Figure 3A).

claim: 414 genes were categorized as SIRT2 independent.
source: Genes that remained unaltered after AGK2 treatment were categorized as SIRT2 independent (414 genes) and the rest as SIRT2 dependent (578 genes) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis (Figure 3A).

claim: A significant number of pathways that are known to play a crucial role in combating TB were affected by AGK2 treatment.
source: KEGG pathway analysis on SIRT2-dependent genes belonging to these groups (expect group 5) revealed that a significant number of pathways that are known to play a crucial role in combating TB were affected by AGK2 treatment (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by KEGG pathway analysis (Figure 3B).

claim: Genes involved in antigen presentation were significantly upregulated in SIRT2 inhibited samples.
source: For instance, genes involved in antigen presentation, Th17 cell differentiation, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, NF-κB signaling, tuberculosis, etc were significantly upregulated while PI3K/Akt signaling pathway was downregulated in SIRT2 inhibited samples (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by KEGG pathway analysis (Figure 3B).

claim: Genes involved in Th17 cell differentiation were significantly upregulated in SIRT2 inhibited samples.
source: For instance, genes involved in antigen presentation, Th17 cell differentiation, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, NF-κB signaling, tuberculosis, etc were significantly upregulated while PI3K/Akt signaling pathway was downregulated in SIRT2 inhibited samples (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by KEGG pathway analysis (Figure 3B).

claim: PI3K/Akt signaling pathway was downregulated in SIRT2 inhibited samples.
source: For instance, genes involved in antigen presentation, Th17 cell differentiation, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, NF-κB signaling, tuberculosis, etc were significantly upregulated while PI3K/Akt signaling pathway was downregulated in SIRT2 inhibited samples (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by KEGG pathway analysis (Figure 3B).

claim: The expression of genes involved in T cell activation was enhanced in SIRT2-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, the expression of genes involved in T cell activation was enhanced in SIRT2-dependent manner (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq data showing heatmap of T cell activation genes (Figure 3C).

claim: Mtb hijacks host SIRT2 to rewire the host transcriptional landscape for its survival.
source: These results reiterate the existence of a novel anti-defense strategy employed by Mtb wherein it hijacks host SIRT2 to rewire the host transcriptional landscape for its survival.
evidence: Inferred from RNAseq data showing SIRT2-dependent gene expression changes (Figure 3).

claim: SIRT2 inhibition led to a marked increase in the expression of monocyte differentiation markers CD11b and CD11c.
source: SIRT2 inhibition led to a marked increase in the expression of monocyte differentiation markers, CD11b and CD11c (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4B–D).

claim: AGK2 treatment resulted in the increased expression of MHCII and CD80 co-stimulatory molecules.
source: AGK2 treatment resulted in the increased expression of MHCII and CD80 co-stimulatory molecules which are known to stimulate T cells (Figure 4B, E and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4B, E and F).

claim: MHCII and CD80 co-stimulatory molecules are known to stimulate T cells.
source: AGK2 treatment resulted in the increased expression of MHCII and CD80 co-stimulatory molecules which are known to stimulate T cells (Figure 4B, E and F).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about co-stimulatory molecules.

claim: The expression of CD11b, CD11c, CD80 and MHCII was significantly increased when only T cells were pre-treated with AGK2.
source: Interestingly, the expression of CD11b, CD11c and co-stimulatory markers CD80 and MHCII was significantly increased even in the condition where only the T cells were pre-treated with AGK2 (Figure 4B–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4B–F).

claim: There was no change in the percentage of CD4+ T cells upon AGK2 treatment.
source: With no change in the percentage of CD4+ T cells (Figure 4G and H), we observed an increase in their activation as evidenced by an increased expression of T cell activation markers CD69 and CD25 (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4G and H).

claim: An increase in CD4+ T cell activation was observed as evidenced by increased expression of T cell activation markers CD69 and CD25.
source: With no change in the percentage of CD4+ T cells (Figure 4G and H), we observed an increase in their activation as evidenced by an increased expression of T cell activation markers CD69 and CD25 (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4I and J).

claim: A similar trend of increased activation was observed in CD8+ T cells.
source: A similar trend was observed in CD8+ T cells (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4K–M).

claim: SIRT2 inhibition increased the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines IFNγ and IL17 by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Furthermore, SIRT2 inhibition increased the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines IFNγ and IL17 by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 4N–Q).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4N–Q).

claim: SIRT2 inhibition in macrophage alone failed to drive strong Th1 and Th17 responses in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: However, SIRT2 inhibition in macrophage alone failed to drive strong Th1 and Th17 responses in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells while co-treatment of macrophages and T cells with AGK2 had a synergistic effect as IFNγ and IL17 production was significantly higher when splenocytes were co-cultured with macrophages in the presence of AGK2 (Figure 4N–Q).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4N–Q).

claim: Co-treatment of macrophages and T cells with AGK2 had a synergistic effect on IFNγ and IL17 production.
source: However, SIRT2 inhibition in macrophage alone failed to drive strong Th1 and Th17 responses in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells while co-treatment of macrophages and T cells with AGK2 had a synergistic effect as IFNγ and IL17 production was significantly higher when splenocytes were co-cultured with macrophages in the presence of AGK2 (Figure 4N–Q).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4N–Q).

claim: Treatment of AGK2 in splenocytes alone or in both cell types led to significantly higher reduction in bacterial survival compared to SIRT2 inhibition in macrophages alone.
source: Similarly, the treatment of AGK2 in splenocytes alone or in both the cell types led to a significantly higher reduction in bacterial survival as compared to the SIRT2 inhibition in macrophages alone (Figure 4R).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU enumeration (Figure 4R).

claim: SIRT2 plays a role in modulating host protective T cell responses.
source: Overall, these results implicate a role for SIRT2 in modulating host protective T cell responses.
evidence: Inferred from data showing effects of SIRT2 inhibition on T cell activation and cytokine production (Figure 4).

claim: A significantly increased expression of SIRT2 was observed in CD3+ lymphocytes isolated from the spleen of Mtb-infected animals.
source: Interestingly, we observed a significantly increased expression of SIRT2 in CD3+ lymphocytes isolated from the spleen of Mtb-infected animals (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 5B and C).

claim: SIRT2 inhibition by AGK2 modulated the acetylation levels of H3K18 in CD3+ lymphocytes.
source: Replicating the profile obtained in Mtb-infected macrophages, SIRT2 inhibition by AGK2 modulated the acetylation levels of H3K18 in these cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 5D).

claim: Histopathology analysis of infected lungs showed an overall decrease in lung inflammation after SIRT2 inhibition.
source: Histopathology analysis of infected lungs showed an overall decrease in lung inflammation after SIRT2 inhibition (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis (Figure 6B–D).

claim: The bacterial burden was significantly diminished in the lungs, spleen and liver of mice treated with AGK2 as compared with the control mice.
source: These data were further strengthened by the CFU analysis wherein the bacterial burden was significantly diminished in the lungs, spleen and liver of mice treated with AGK2 as compared with the control mice (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU enumeration (Figure 6E–G).

claim: AGK2 treatment in Rag1-/- mice did not alter the bacterial survival as compared to the control group.
source: AGK2 treatment in these immunodeficient mice did not alter the bacterial survival as compared to the control group (Figure 6H–J) indicating that SIRT2 inhibition in T cells is indispensable in restricting Mtb growth inside the host.
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU enumeration in Rag1-/- mice (Figure 6H–J).

claim: SIRT2 inhibition in T cells is indispensable in restricting Mtb growth inside the host.
source: AGK2 treatment in these immunodeficient mice did not alter the bacterial survival as compared to the control group (Figure 6H–J) indicating that SIRT2 inhibition in T cells is indispensable in restricting Mtb growth inside the host.
evidence: Inferred from data showing no effect of AGK2 in Rag1-/- mice (Figure 6H–J).

claim: Increased percentage of CD11b+, CD11c+, CD80+ and MHCII+ cells was observed in the lungs of AGK2-treated mice.
source: Increased percentage of CD11b+, CD11c+, CD80+ and MHCII+ cells, which are involved in the stimulation of adaptive immune responses, was observed in the lungs (Figure 7A–E) and the spleen of AGK2-treated mice (7F-7I).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 7A–E).

claim: Increased percentage of CD11b+, CD11c+, CD80+ and MHCII+ cells was observed in the spleen of AGK2-treated mice.
source: Increased percentage of CD11b+, CD11c+, CD80+ and MHCII+ cells, which are involved in the stimulation of adaptive immune responses, was observed in the lungs (Figure 7A–E) and the spleen of AGK2-treated mice (7F-7I).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 7F–I).

claim: CD11b+, CD11c+, CD80+ and MHCII+ cells are involved in the stimulation of adaptive immune responses.
source: Increased percentage of CD11b+, CD11c+, CD80+ and MHCII+ cells, which are involved in the stimulation of adaptive immune responses, was observed in the lungs (Figure 7A–E) and the spleen of AGK2-treated mice (7F-7I).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about these cell surface markers.

claim: An increased activation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was observed in the lungs of infected animals after AGK2 treatment.
source: Similar to our ex vivo results, we observed an increased activation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the lungs (Figure 8A–G) and the spleen (Figure 8H–M) of infected animals after AGK2 treatment.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 8A–G).

claim: An increased activation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was observed in the spleen of infected animals after AGK2 treatment.
source: Similar to our ex vivo results, we observed an increased activation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the lungs (Figure 8A–G) and the spleen (Figure 8H–M) of infected animals after AGK2 treatment.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 8H–M).

claim: The Th1 and Th17 bias in the immune response was evidenced by a prominent increase in the population of IFNγ and IL17 producing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the lungs of AGK2-treated mice.
source: Moreover, the Th1 and Th17 bias in the immune response was evidenced by a prominent increase in the population of INFγ and IL17 producing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the lungs of AGK2-treated mice (Figure 9A–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 9A–E).

claim: CD3+ cells isolated from the lungs of AGK2 treated and Mtb-infected mice displayed enhanced levels of NFκB p65 acetylation.
source: Interestingly, CD3+ cells isolated from the lungs of AGK2 treated and Mtb-infected mice displayed enhanced levels of NFκB p65 acetylation (Figure 9F and G).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 9F and G).

claim: An increase in the percentage of splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells producing pro-inflammatory cytokines IFNγ and IL17 was observed upon SIRT2 inhibition.
source: Upon SIRT2 inhibition, we observed a similar increase in the percentage of splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells producing pro-inflammatory cytokines IFNγ and IL17 (Figure 9H–K), indicating a shift in the immune balance toward Th1 and Th17 response.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 9H–K).

claim: SIRT2 inhibition indicates a shift in the immune balance toward Th1 and Th17 response.
source: Upon SIRT2 inhibition, we observed a similar increase in the percentage of splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells producing pro-inflammatory cytokines IFNγ and IL17 (Figure 9H–K), indicating a shift in the immune balance toward Th1 and Th17 response.
evidence: Inferred from data showing increased IFNγ and IL17 production (Figure 9H–K).

claim: AGK2 treatment had no effect on the apoptotic levels in the splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: We observed that AGK2 treatment had no effect on the apoptotic levels in the splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 10B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Annexin V staining and flow cytometry (Figure 10B and C).

claim: ROS levels were similar in the CD4+ and CD8+ T cells isolated from the spleen of infected and AGK2 treated animals.
source: Similarly, ROS levels were also similar in the CD4+ and CD8+ T cells isolated from the spleen of infected and AGK2 treated animals (Figure 10D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by CellROX staining and flow cytometry (Figure 10D and E).

claim: Mycobacterial growth was significantly restricted in macrophages co-cultured with T cells isolated from AGK2-treated mice.
source: Interestingly, mycobacterial growth was significantly restricted in macrophages co-cultured with T cells isolated from AGK2-treated mice (Figure 10F) indicating that AGK2 treatment enhances the efficacy of T cells in terms of stimulating macrophages for efficient bacterial clearance.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 10F).

claim: AGK2 treatment enhances the efficacy of T cells in terms of stimulating macrophages for efficient bacterial clearance.
source: Interestingly, mycobacterial growth was significantly restricted in macrophages co-cultured with T cells isolated from AGK2-treated mice (Figure 10F) indicating that AGK2 treatment enhances the efficacy of T cells in terms of stimulating macrophages for efficient bacterial clearance.
evidence: Inferred from data showing restricted mycobacterial growth in co-culture experiments (Figure 10F).

claim: T cells from AGK2-treated animals were more efficient in imparting protection to Rag1-/- mice compared to T cells from Mtb-infected mice.
source: Furthermore, T cells from AGK2-treated animals were more efficient in imparting protection to the Rag1-/- mice as compared to the T cells from Mtb-infected mice (Cnt) (Figure 10G and H).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU enumeration in adoptive transfer experiments (Figure 10G and H).

claim: AGK2 treatment significantly lowered the bacterial load in the lungs, spleen and liver of infected BALB/c animals.
source: AGK2 treatment significantly lowered the bacterial load in the lungs (Figure 11B), spleen (Figure 11C) and liver (Figure 11D) of infected animals as compared to the control group.
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU enumeration (Figure 11B–D).

claim: Co-treatment of AGK2 and INH significantly decreased the bacterial burden in the lungs as compared to mice treated with either AGK2 or INH alone.
source: Co-treatment of AGK2 and INH significantly decreased the bacterial burden in the lungs as compared to the mice treated with either AGK2 or INH alone (Figure 11F).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU enumeration (Figure 11F).

claim: AGK2 treatment significantly decreased the bacillary load of MDR strains of TB.
source: Interestingly, AGK2 treatment significantly decreased the bacillary load of MDR as well as XDR strains of TB (Figure 11G–I).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU enumeration (Figure 11G–I).

claim: AGK2 treatment significantly decreased the bacillary load of XDR strains of TB.
source: Interestingly, AGK2 treatment significantly decreased the bacillary load of MDR as well as XDR strains of TB (Figure 11G–I).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU enumeration (Figure 11G–I).

claim: One of the advantages of host-directed therapies (HDTs) is the reduction in the risk of generation of drug resistance.
source: One of the advantages of host-directed therapies (HDTs) is the reduction in the risk of generation of drug resistance.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about host-directed therapies.

claim: HDTs provide untapped opportunities to eliminate drug-resistant strains by manipulating host immune system.
source: HDTs provide untapped opportunities to eliminate drug-resistant strains by manipulating host immune system.

claim: Tuberculosis (TB) is a deadly disease caused by the intracellular pathogen Mtb.
source: Tuberculosis (TB), a deadly disease caused by the intracellular pathogen Mtb, has existed since time immemorial and continues to remain one of the leading causes of mortality by a single infectious agent (WHO, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2018.

claim: TB continues to remain one of the leading causes of mortality by a single infectious agent.
source: Tuberculosis (TB), a deadly disease caused by the intracellular pathogen Mtb, has existed since time immemorial and continues to remain one of the leading causes of mortality by a single infectious agent (WHO, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2018.

claim: Classic anti-TB therapy fails to provide complete sterilization in the host.
source: Classic anti-TB therapy which comprises the administration of multiple anti-mycobacterial drugs, fails to provide complete sterilization in the host.
